title: The wheel the earth held
hookLine: Karna's wheel sinks and his weapon slips away, as two old deeds come due
carry: karma: even an accident bears fruit
tomorrow: Karna calls out to wait. will anyone listen?

cards: Karna and Arjuna, at last, face to face. Karna fits a terrible arrow to his bow, an arrow with a serpent in it, the epic says, a snake with an old grudge against Arjuna.
Shalya, at the reins, gives him advice: aim for the chest. Karna refuses. He doesn't aim twice, he says, and he looses at Arjuna's head.

And Krishna, driving the other chariot, presses down with his feet, and the chariot sinks into the earth, just enough. The serpent arrow takes Arjuna's crown and leaves Arjuna alive. Hold on to that sinking chariot.

teach.b: The duel goes on, and then the earth takes hold of Karna's chariot wheel. It sinks, and it stays sunk. In the same moment Karna reaches in memory for his greatest weapon, and the words are gone.
The epic explains both with old deeds.
Years before, Karna had killed a Brahmin's cow by accident, and the Brahmin cursed him: when you most need it, the earth will swallow your wheel.
And as a young man Karna had trained under the great teacher Parashurama, hiding who he was. When the teacher found out, he cursed him to forget that weapon in the hour he needed it.
Two old debts, come due on one afternoon. The earth that saved Arjuna now holds Karna fast.

teach.h: KARMA: EVERY ACT IS A SEED
teach.b: Hindus call it karma: every act is a seed, and it ripens in its own time. Karna never meant to kill that cow, and the fruit came anyway. Intention matters, and Hindu teachers weigh it, but an act still leaves its mark.
That's one reason many pujas end with a short prayer asking pardon for anything done wrong, knowingly or unknowingly.

teach.h: PARDON FOR WHAT WE DIDN'T MEAN
teach.b: Not guilt for its own sake: a habit of owning even the harm you didn't mean. Karna jumps down and grips the wheel with both hands: the commander of an army, on foot, straining at a wheel.

how: Many Hindu pujas close with a short prayer asking pardon for any fault done knowingly or unknowingly. The scene of Karna on foot, straining to lift his sunken wheel, is retold in recitations, plays and serials of the Mahabharata, along with the curses behind it.

o: the archer whose crown the serpent arrow carries off
the teacher who curses a student for hiding his birth
the commander whose wheel sinks and whose weapon slips away

games.q: two old deeds — tap the pairs.
p: pressed his chariot into the earth

s: Karna's wheel stuck by plain bad luck
the epic ties it to a curse for a cow Karna killed by accident: an old act, ripening.
in Hindu teaching, an act done by accident leaves no mark at all
intention matters, but every act is a seed; Karna's accident still came due.
many pujas end by asking pardon for wrongs done knowingly or unknowingly
a habit of owning even the harm you didn't mean.

games.q: you bump a classmate's project and crack it. nobody saw, and you didn't mean to. by what Karna's wheel teaches, what fits?
o: tell them and help fix it; an accident still leaves a mark.
say nothing; no intention, no karma.
blame the table it was sitting on.
games.why: Karna never meant to kill the cow, and the fruit still came. Hindus own even unmeant harm, which is why the pardon prayer covers what was done unknowingly.

practice: Sit tall, both feet on the floor. Let one small harm come to mind that you never meant: a careless word, a forgotten promise, a moment you weren't paying attention.

If you pray, ask pardon for it in your own words, and for the ones you don't know about, the way many Hindus close their worship. If you don't pray, simply own it to yourself, and choose one small way to make it right.

wordCard.voice: Karna. The warrior whose wheel sinks and whose weapon slips from memory, when two old deeds come due on one afternoon.
